title: Apps
subtitle: The apps on your phone are one of the biggest sources of data collection in your life. This guide covers the popular privacy-respecting alternatives for messaging, email, file transfer, and finance.

context.title: What to look for in an app
context.body: Before installing any app, ask yourself: Does it use end-to-end encryption (e2ee)? Does it have a clear privacy policy? Does it have a business model that doesn't rely on selling user data?
context.body2: A free app with no obvious revenue source is almost certainly monetizing you. As they say, if something's free, then you're the product.

items.name: Switch to an end-to-end encrypted (e2ee) messaging
items.why: SMS messages pass through your phone carrier's servers in plain text, meaning they aren't encrypted (this is not the case for iMessage or RCS messaging). WhatsApp uses e2ee for message content but its metadata (who you talk to, when, how often) is still shared with Meta.

steps.text: `Signal` - the gold standard for e2ee messaging. Open source, independently audited, zero metadata retention. Best choice for most people. Download from `signal.org/download` only
`Threema` - doesn't require a phone number. Sign up anonymously with a randomly generated ID. Swiss-based, audited. ~$5 one-time purchase
`Session` - decentralized, no phone number or email required. Routes messages through a distributed network - no central server to subpoena
`Briar` - designed for high-risk scenarios. Works over Tor, Bluetooth, or Wi-Fi without internet. Best for activists. Android only

items.name: Switch to a privacy-focused email provider
items.path: Replaces Gmail, Yahoo, Outlook for sensitive use
items.why: Google scans Gmail content to serve targeted ads and complies with law enforcement data requests. Your inbox likely contains years of sensitive documents - account statements, medical correspondence, legal notices. A zero-knowledge email provider means even the provider cannot read your messages.

steps.text: `ProtonMail` - Swiss-based, e2ee, free tier available. Most popular privacy email. Sign up at `mail.proton.me`
`Startmail` - Netherlands-based, PGP encryption, supports custom domains. Focused exclusively on email privacy
`Firefox Relay` - email masking service. Generates disposable relay addresses that forward to your real inbox. Real address never exposed to senders. Free tier available at `relay.firefox.com`
`Apple Hide My Email` (iCloud+) - creates random relay addresses on the fly when signing up for services. Seamless on Apple devices
Use `Emailnator` or `10minutemail.com` for throwaway inboxes when you just need a one-time confirmation email
Delete sensitive documents from your inbox after downloading. Google was found to be scanning the content of users' Gmail accounts

items.name: Use virtual cards for online purchases
items.path: privacy.com - replaces real card number for online spending
items.why: When you use your real credit or debit card online, you're handing that card number to every merchant you buy from. A single breach at any merchant exposes your real financial details. Virtual card services generate a unique card number per merchant - if that number is leaked, only that card is compromised, not your real account.

steps.text: Sign up at `privacy.com` and link your bank account or debit card. The free tier gives you up to 12 virtual cards per month
When making an online purchase, generate a new virtual card in the Privacy.com app or browser extension
Set a spending limit on each card - e.g. a $15/month cap on a streaming subscription prevents unexpected charges
For subscription services you want to try, create a single-use card - it works once then automatically closes, making it impossible for the merchant to charge you again
Also audit your Venmo privacy settings - Venmo transactions are public by default. Go to `Settings → Privacy` and set all transactions to `Private`

items.name: Use secure file transfer for sensitive documents
items.path: Replaces Google Drive links, email attachments, Dropbox
items.why: When you share a file via Google Drive or Dropbox, a copy lives on their servers potentially indefinitely and is subject to subpoena. Secure transfer tools send files directly between sender and recipient, encrypted in transit, with no persistent server-side copy.

steps.text: `Wormhole` (wormhole.app) - encrypted file transfer up to 10GB. Files are available for 24 hours then automatically deleted. No account required
`OnionShare` - routes file transfers over the Tor network. Ideal for journalists and activists sharing sensitive documents anonymously. Can also host anonymous websites
How to use Wormhole: go to `wormhole.app`, drag your file onto the page, send the generated link via Signal or another E2EE messenger
Send the link via Signal or another E2EE messenger - not email or SMS

items.name: Use a period tracker that stores data locally only
items.path: Replaces Flo, Clue, Stardust, and most mainstream trackers
items.why: Period tracking data can reveal pregnancy, miscarriage, and reproductive health information. In the post-Roe legal landscape, there is documented concern that this data could be subpoenaed or purchased by state prosecutors. Most mainstream period apps - including Flo and Stardust - have been found to share data with third parties despite privacy claims.

steps.text: `Euki` - designed specifically for reproductive health privacy. All data stored locally on your device. Open source. Free. iOS and Android
`Drip` - open source cycle tracker with no cloud sync. Includes a duress password feature to hide data if your phone is searched. iOS and Android
Avoid `Flo` - agreed to FTC settlement after sharing health data with Facebook and Google despite privacy promises
Avoid `Stardust` - claimed end-to-end encryption but was found to share user phone numbers with third parties
Disable health app integrations with Apple Health or Google Fit for any period tracker - this prevents data from being shared with those platforms

items.name: High-risk apps
items.path: App Library → swipe or long press to delete
items.why: All of these apps have demonstrated behaviors that warrant additional research before downloading to your personal device. Temu, for example, elevates its permissions to grant it unrestricted admin access in such a way that security researchers have likened it to malware. Others, like DeepSeek, were found to be sending unencrypted sensitive user information back to their servers. Health and wellness apps collect a lot of sensitive user information then many of them sell it to data brokers.

steps.text: `Temu` - a lawsuit described it as 'dangerous malware.' Requests access to camera, microphone, location, contacts, and file storage. Sends data to servers in China, which some people worry is accessible by the Chinese government
`DeepSeek` - security researchers found hardcoded encryption keys and poor security practices
`TikTok` - ByteDance (parent company) is subject to Chinese national security laws requiring data cooperation with authorities
`mental health apps` - Mozilla's Privacy Not Included project found a majority of apps they checked failed basic security and privacy standards, sharing therapy session data with third parties
`free VPN apps` (except Proton VPN's free tier) - many free VPNs monetize by selling your browsing data. Facebook's Onavo VPN was used to wiretap competitor app usage
Audit any unused apps: on iPhone go to `Settings → Privacy & Security` and review camera, microphone, and location permissions
